title: AI-Enabled Organisations: From Strategy to Practice

segments.text: Welcome to our last and final session for today. Uh AI enabled organizations from strategy to practice. So basically we close the day where every
transformation either succeeds or quietly dies. Uh the gap between strategy and practice. So leading our final session uh is Damiana Casil uh the director people business partner at
Dojons co-speaker Lars Roger CEO uh generally Deutseland Bendict Hook also the head of AI at Kabmk and last but not least Chris Den chief
technology officer at Criteria. Please welcome our final panel for today. >> More is Yeah. Thanks. Thanks. We're nearly there. Last session, everyone. Great. Okay, let's get into it. So, uh the
session is titled from strategy to practice. And I want to start with a quick temperature check. On a scale of 1 to 10, how production ready is AI inside
your organization today? One number each and then tell us what's behind it. And I'll start with you, Chris. >> All right. Hello everyone. My name is
Chris. I'm the chief technology and AI officer at Criteria. Our organization is I'll be aggressive here and say a nine on the 10point scale. We're a less than
200 employee organization headquartered in Los Angeles in California. And we have no choice but to be on the bleeding edge because the world is filled with
unstructured data in the hiring world. And in order to make the best hires and have the most predictive talent engine, we must have our own fine-tuned models
deployed at scale. We must push the boundaries of how we measure those talent signals and uh we take a lot of pride in that and we push very very hard
on the edge. >> Okay, Benedict, what about you? >> Super. So also great to be joining you. I'm Benedict um running AI for KPG
Germany in the IMA region. On the one hand side, I'm supporting clients with their AI transformation. On the other hand side in Lima region we have 160,000
employees that also need to work with AI and are part of the AI journey. I would give it a bit differentiated a 10 for
everybody having access a nine for 90% using AI at least every day and maybe a seven or eight for the ones who really use it in a transformative way because
some are still like just using it as a tool and a >> okay three numbers there but but okay. Okay. And uh what about you Lars?
>> Um so thanks for the question. I'm L Rocka. I'm the CEO of Generali in Germany. Um I would score our organization at a 7.5 or eight. I think
we're doing a very good job, but let's be also humble. The insurance industry is usually not the tech leader for the sector. I think we're are welldeveloped.
We're projecting savings in Germany about 100 million euros uh run rate from next year on through AI in the different areas. We're activating the
organization, but you're never there where you want to be. So, I would say let's stay humble. Seven and a half to eight. >> I like that. And I'm staying with you,
Lars. Insurance runs on decades old core systems. So, when you move an AI model from sandbox to production, what's the hardest integration layer? Is it the
data pipelines, the legacy APIs, the compliance signoff process, or maybe something else that it entirely surprised you? >> That's a good question. And for me, the
learning of the last years, and I've been in different companies over the last years, is really, it is not so much the tech stack. The tech stack, you
know, you know that you're with legacy systems. It's a matter of time. It's a matter of APIs. It's a matter of money. It's about execution. It's for me on the
one hand the change management that you have to get of course in the regulated industry the governance layer on top that you have to manage the different
parts of the organization the risk management and get the business buy in and then the key part actually to be successful is that you need to create a
lighthouse somewhere not too easy case that you can use then to really drive this organization have a pull instead a push not a pull instead of a push that
you really have the your colleagues wanting to get onto this journey. So, it's a lot about change management. The tech part is difficult, but you know
where it's at and you can manage it with time and money. >> But a follow up on that cuz regulated industries often require explanability.
So, has that constraint actually improved your engineering discipline or does it just slow everything down? Now of course we are sticking to the regul regulatory parts and I think as
you point out a very important part banking and insurance as a highly regulated industry. So you you of course have your document everything. You need
a control pane and so forth. You cannot afford to have everybody just using any prompt that they want. But you put a governance on top of this. You control
this. You document. So it is absolutely feasible. You can use this in the underwriting process. You can have this in the leakage and payout process. And
of course also in the efficiency but of course in a regulated industry like the financial services it is one of the key attention points that you have to manage
changing industry entirely. Chris you build AI products that make consequential decisions about people. Walk us through what your deployment pipeline looks like when a single model
update could introduce bias at scale. >> It's a really ch it's a really big challenge. I think when you think about hiring, it's very important to know that
there are consequences to a model that makes the wrong decisions. And it's also really important to understand that in hiring, we believe in a human at the
center approach where AI is a data point in the process, but humans are ultimately making the best hiring decisions. And our goal is not to remove
the human from that process, but to augment and amplify the human skill that's involved in the art of hiring and add a bit of science to it. So we've
made a series of bets the last 3 years building our what we call AI core, our AI infrastructure. We bet pretty heavily on open-source infrastructure,
infrastructure that we can control. We were concerned about model lock. We were concerned about rapid changing in availability and pricing and model suns setting. We have processed more than 80
million assessments around the world in 20 plus languages. And if we were to have an interruption in a frontier model, it is not enough lead time for us
to be able to prepare a new model for the candidate pools that are currently being interviewed or assessed. So for us that strategy was key to how we scaled.
We also when we talk about transparency and hiring being a regulated space, it's critical that every year we conduct adverse impact studies, we conduct bias
audits. We have to make sure our models have the highest level of transparency as they're built. And we also need to make sure that the data going into those
models limits the impact of bias in the hiring process. So our pipeline is very sophisticated. It has to be in order to achieve the quality of outcome we're
looking for in hiring. >> And Benedict, you advise dozens of companies on AI rollouts. So what's the most common architectural mistake you see organizations make when they move
from proof of concept to production? I would like to share two things and the one is very connected to what you just said. So I think when you do a proof of
concept or proof of value, it's often a very limited scope and environment not connected to the real systems, processes, etc. So doing that proof of
concept is relatively easy. In particular, when you consider how you can do wipe coding and all of that stuff today, it's rather easy to run a huge
number also of proof of concepts. But when you consider all these surroundings like you need to ground it into your platforms, you need to adjust processes
and particular when you work with agents um you need to do the uh change management component to really ensure that people are prepared for it and use
it later on. Um and that's where it really gets tricky. then suddenly AI is moving fast but you are grounded into slow release cycles for example etc etc
so I think while doing the proof of concept you still need to consider readiness of the surroundings to really make sure that you get not caught and
the other one is that if you talk to companies nowadays like every company will tell you we have 500 a thousand use cases but that's not the discussion
anymore really and what some companies struggle a bit with is they still think in these isolated boxes of use cases in a way and then you will never achieve
scalability in a way. You need to think about basically redesigning your processes or at least you need to think in reusable capabilities. One example is
if you do customer service center automation, HR service automation, IT help desk automation. It's basically the same pattern of capabilities you need and you only want to build it once and
reusable many times. And because companies are not doing that sometimes also the value calculation does not work because they think in isolated boxes. Yes. And talking about that I'd like to
touch a little bit on the engineering reality and developers experience and um Lars at general scale you have thousands of employees who aren't engineers.
Actually I met a few of the team last night. they've been at the company for a very very long time. Um, but now they
need to interact with AI powered tools daily. So what does internal enablement actually look like? >> I think there is two important components. On the one hand side, you
have the content and the generation by experienced central teams. But as I said before, it's changing the organization is key for us. It's really activating
the organization. So what we are implementing currently as a pilot and will roll out over entire Germany is what we call an AI buddy concept. We
will have 45 young colleagues. We call them young lions who are trained actually and then train their other colleagues. They will go around the
offices peer-to-peer training and try to give give help with co-pilot and so forth. It's not about generating the perfect prompt. It's giving some advice
to make people familiar with the technology and taking the fear because of course in most industries it's also not just the chance is being seen but
also the fear is seen of is it about jobs what can I do and so forth and we have some good experience with some
young guys and so 45 people are currently being trained and then we will roll out in the customer service centers and they will train their colleagues to
really get them acquainted with the basic tools also maybe some clo uh uh training and so forth, but we will focus strongly on co-pilot in the beginning.
Like I said, it's not about a perfection. It's about peer-to-peer training to colleagues. And so far, the experiences are very good. >> I like that. And Chris, as a CTO hiring
engineers, has Genai changed what good looks like in a technical interview? And are you testing for different skills? >> I talk a lot about work 4.0, work 4.0.
Um you can kind of summarize the trajectory there of work 1.0 being kind of industrial revolution, work 2.0 being uh you know a corporate era, work 3.0
being digitalization, and work 4.0 now being the combination of humans and agents at work. And in our data across tens of millions of assessments and
seeing this data every day, what we're seeing is that an emphasis on resilience, aptitude, cognitive ability, um, frankly, emotional intelligence, your ability to be adaptive. Those were
often called, uh, soft skills, and we've rebranded those to durable skills. And we're seeing that those durable skills are more important than ever when it
comes to the work 4.0 era. And when I look for engineers, particularly in the way we solve challenges today, we have bias towards engineers who are excellent
at the thought process, the critical thinking, the solving, the resilience, the ability to adapt. Um, of course there's foundational hard skill that you can't ignore. You need people who have
understanding of the true uh goals of engineering. But it's a surprise as many of you might feel that the re-emphasis on durable skills which are less
technical are actually at the forefront of building the best engineers in this era. >> I'm going to steal that one because in my company we absolutely hate the world
the word soft skills. So durable skills, it's a much much better way to put it and it's music to my ears as a as a HR
professional. And Benedict, I'm curious, are you seeing evidence that AI coding tools genuinely improve throughput or are senior engineers increasingly spending their time reviewing and fixing
AI gener generated code? So I think one uh definite advantage of AI coding is that it's not only about the coding itself but it basically
changes the full life cycle of how you introduce and develop software. For example, what I find in particular really valuable is like let's say in the
past you had like a requirements engineering conceptual phase and this is really fundamentally being changed because you can more or less instantly create like a prototype of uh the system
you are creating and you really discuss facts in the end and you speed that up. So I find that to be really valuable and
you might even create like a first mockup you will potentially not reuse but it still gives you a lot of speed and focus in your requirements phase in
a way. So it's much more outcome based today than it was before. And then I think it's it's not just the senior and junior discussion. I also believe that a
junior today needs to have more skills than just doing the code. They need to have judgment. I liked your your skill description. They need to be able to do
reviews. They are much more like an orchestrator. But I also believe skills like storytelling are more important for developers nowadays because you can really speed up the cycle. And in
particular when you are doing the introduction of let's say a standard system such as Salesforce, SAP, service now whatsoever they all integrate uh agents that do the actual customization
and coding into the platform. And by utilizing that really the initial phase is much faster, much more focused and you more or less directly can discuss
some outputs. So it's changing overall putting much more focus on like what do you really want to achieve and how do you test it, review it and make sure it
does what it should do. >> And now let's be a little bit um let's look at what kills AI strategies. And Lars, you've run large scales operations
first at Aliens Partners and now at General Ali. When transformation stalls, is it typically a technical bottleneck or a political one? And how do we
unblock it? >> So I would say it's usually not a technical because as I said in the initial question, technical issues you can overcome. We have the technology.
It's about implementation. You can schedule it. Of course, it's not easy, but it's a plannable and if you know your shop, you know what's to come.
Political, it's a it's for me is a matter of change management. So, on the one hand, I think you need somebody who really feels accountable. You have to
have somebody in the top management and also in the levels below that is accountable. Is it me as the COO? Yes. But also it goes beyond because it's not
just a technical transformation. It's the business concept. If you're using AI, the sales guys need to be on board. The product owners need to be on board.
So it has to be a change process of the organization. And then I think in order to convince them after this political buy in ownership, it's it's it's about
building a lighthouse. And from my experience, it was really we build a lighthouse. We took in my old role one country. We took use cases that were not
easy. It took us then 3 months longer, but we we build it up. It worked and we could show in a global organization to
the other entities and stakeholders it was working. So it was not again anymore the group s COO wants it. There was a demand to meet my customer centricity
targets and my my cost targets. And with this lighthouse, we generated this pull approach. And by that, frankly spoken within 2 years conversational AI, we
built a voice bot that had 10 million voice bot minutes. And in the next phase brought it up to 20 million voicebot minutes where in the beginning people
said we would be crazy because it had really we could prove customer centricity. If there's netcat, people will be open. They want a fast service
and it was efficient for the company and it was working. So you had all on board. Right. And Benedict, you must have seen AI strategies die. So when a well-funded
and well-intentioned AI program collapse, what's the actual cause of death? >> I think uh first of all, it's important to know that there's not uh like one AI
strategy that takes you from zero to full transformation, but it has different stages. And the questions in the the beginning are more often like
how do you we introduce like first productivity boosters such as co-pilot, how do we create an initial governance? How do we train our people? How do we
create opportunities that they can work with AI etc etc but after you completed that phase you typically move more towards transformation like rethinking processes
uh from like stepby-step things made for humans more into capability based models. uh change gets more important, the people perspective gets much more important and after completing that many
companies start to also think about improving business models or changing business models. But what's is important like the initial phase that's rather simple for companies because you have
these isolated things like introducing co-pilot, introducing training to drive that. But as soon as you move towards transformation and really changing, it's like everybody has a stake in that. uh
technology, people, governance etc etc and you cannot drive that in isolation but it really needs to be an integrated approach through the transformation. This can also not be delegated. So you
very often really need like the top leaders driving that uh hand in hand and and integrated to make sure that in the end you achieve the transformed output.
And I think the point where you move from foundations to transformation, that's a point that's typically very hard for companies to make that transition. Um and there it often
breaks. >> And Chris, you've built and scaled multiple tech companies. What's one non-obvious lesson about shipping AI in production that you wish someone had
told you before your first deployment? >> Yeah, it's actually a a fascinating reflection I had while listening to both of you. In the startup world or in the smaller
business mid-market segment, we often have we don't have the luxury of being able to buy all of the tools we always want to buy. I think as an enterprise
there's a level of investment that can be made to experiment, throw things away, uh move. Now you're also navigating a much bigger vessel. So you
know there's pros and cons of course but one of the things that is a key attribute of my world is optimizing for scarcity uh resource-wise. And that
forces us to think differently, particularly about how we might bring coding models into our engineering group. You know, in a perfect world, we'd just be ripping through cloud
tokens uh with an unlimited budget like the rest of the world. But, uh, you know, we have to position ourselves with balance, use open- source tools, open
source harnesses, and there's just a huge emphasis on the strategy there as opposed to having um more resources. So we operate from a perspective of
scarcity. And that's that's something that has really fed me well throughout my career is operating through scarcity. And the second observation I would share
is that if you're conducting a normal transformation in an enterprise or a business and what I mean by normal is maybe the 2000s move uh to a more modern
technology or move to the cloud. there was some visible end point to when you were completing that migration or completing that phase of evolution. And
what we're seeing with AI of course is by the time you get to a point that you might feel content with the goalposts have already moved forward to the next
thing you're working towards. So it's a very fascinating time to be running transformationing companies. Yes, it's it the contrast is is quite striking between between the two worlds.
So, one final question. Um, I'd like you to maybe think and give the audience a couple of concrete actionable things that made AI actually work inside your
organization. So when you've really thought about it from a strategy and then built it into practice, what's an actionable thing that they can take away
from this this discussion? I'll I'll kick us off. Uh so this is advice for product companies because I'm a SAS operator and the cost of operating
services for your product these days uh with AI in your cost of goods is materially different than you know years prior with standard compute and standard
storage costs. And if you're a leader in engineering, uh you may have gotten away in the past of building products without truly recognizing and breaking down the cost
of goods in a particular service. Software as a service has particularly um high margins in general and a lot of times you can solve a problem and not
think about the cost of the software, the cloud etc. while creating that that product. Times have changed. It's amazing when you look at a product that
might cost 1 cent per unit and with a embedded model of various size hosted in your cloud infrastructure could be 100 or 140 times more expensive than what
was standard cloud uh and storage cost. So just something to keep an eye on there when you're building as a SAS product operator or a founder that that
matters. And are you measuring the ROI? >> The the importance of measuring ROI is on how our customers realize that from the platform because we need to be able
to set a target margin on that SAS that a customer will agree with paying and right now across the board vastly in the market most SAS companies are not making
money on their AI products. Right? So um we at criteria are and it's an important calculation we make delivering value to customers while also making sure the
margin is healthy. >> Thank you Lars. What about you? One concrete actionable thing >> I would say on the one hand keep in mind
that you want to scale. So from whatever the solution you want to design keep in mind you want to scale it afterwards. Secondly, don't get into a technological lock in
especially nowadays with the position of Claude. Who would have thought they would be there 3 years ago? Um, and then thirdly, you need to have a clear
ownership. As I said, it's a c it's also a cultural and a business transformations and not just an IT project. So, clear ownership and then
also clear transformational management. Benedict, >> I would uh pick the connection between have like a clear strategic goal and ambition what you would want to achieve
with AI but also manage the people component in the right way. Let me share one example from our own company. In the very beginning we said professional
services is being very much affected and changed by AI and we set ambition three years ago where we said no matter what we do whether it's order tax or advisory
AI is part of everything we do and we have the ambition for everyone at the company to have like a client zero mode. So we want to be fast we want to be bold
we want to share real world learnings from it and everybody has an ownership in that play. This also means that no matter whether someone is like on board
level or just joined the company, everybody has an ownership to be AI literate in a way to learn what it means for their role. And what I mean with get
the people component right to support that obviously you need a lot of uh learning enablement formats, but you also need the right amount of push
whenever push is needed or the right bridge building whenever that is needed in a way. And I think and and last I liked what you said like as soon as you
made your homework on technology foundations giving people access you will very much be stuck in the people discussion around uh transforming organization like who's really taking
the ownership of that do we enable our people. So I think the learning is really have a clear ambition and goal and get the people dimension right.
>> Thank you so much to the three of you. I think as a HR and tech leader the clearest signal from today's discussion is that you can't really buy an AI
enablement or or enabled organization off the shelf. You really have to build it and more importantly you have to build the resilience the culture and the engineering
discipline to support it. So yes, thank you so much uh to you all and I hope you can all enjoy drinks and the rest of
your time at the conference and in Berlin. Thank you. Thank you. Thank you very much.
